e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “figs,” functioning as a noun naming the fruit. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Amos 7:14. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise role in that sentence cannot be described further. Its attested meaning is therefore simple and specific: it identifies figs rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea.

This Hebrew word is a proper name rendered “Bithron,” referring to a specific place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 2:29. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise geographical significance cannot be stated beyond identifying it as the named place Bithron.

The Hebrew word means “Gederite,” a designation identifying someone by association with Geder. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:28. The word functions as an identifying name or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its normal lexical role is to identify a person or group connected with Geder.

“Force” is the clearest supported meaning of this Hebrew word. It refers to force within its single occurrence in the Hebrew Old Testament, found in Ezra 4:23. Since the verse text is not provided here, the word’s precise role in that sentence cannot be described further. Its occurrence is limited to this one reference, so its normal meaning is best understood simply as “force,” without extending it to additional meanings.

This Hebrew word means “bones,” referring to the hard parts of the body. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 6:24, so its normal biblical usage is represented by a single occurrence rather than a broad range of passages. The word identifies physical bones; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain what is being said about them there. Scripture’s use here remains concrete and bodily, not a separate abstract meaning.

The word means “away.” It functions as a verb, telling what happens in relation to being away rather than naming a person, object, or place. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Judges 5:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here. The repeated English rendering supports this basic sense without establishing additional meanings.

Hiddai is a personal name, used to identify an individual rather than to express an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 23:30. English renderings preserve the name as “Hiddai,” so the available information supports recognizing it as a proper name without assigning it an additional meaning or translating it as an ordinary descriptive word.

This Hebrew word means “strange,” describing something outside what is customary or familiar. It appears once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, at Proverbs 21:8. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be expanded beyond this basic meaning. Its use points to something viewed as unfamiliar or not belonging within the expected pattern.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “treasures,” things kept as valuable possessions or reserves. It can describe stored wealth belonging to a person, a king, a nation, or the house of God. The word occurs 79 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing regular use for accumulated wealth and stored goods. Its scriptural connections also place these treasures in settings of giving, receiving, guarding, and dedication, so the word identifies what is held in store rather than the act of storing it.

“Habaiah” is a personal name, referring to an individual or family designation rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. The same name appears in both passages, showing its use as an identifying name. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or family being listed there.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of being “strong.” It refers to strength or firmness as a quality, rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, and Daniel. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its consistent central idea is strength: something or someone possessing power, firmness, or might. The word is found in 2 Chronicles 12:1; 2 Chronicles 26:16; Isaiah 8:11; and Daniel 11:2.

This Hebrew word describes people as “armed”—equipped and ready for military action. It functions as a description of those prepared to serve in battle, rather than naming a weapon itself. In the Old Testament, it occurs 44 times, especially in passages concerning organized forces and those prepared to go out. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains being armed and ready.

This Hebrew noun means “court,” naming a court rather than describing an action or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, and its sole recorded occurrence is Isaiah 34:13. The word therefore identifies a place or area called a court in that passage. Its precise role in Isaiah 34:13 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here. This is a rare Hebrew word in the biblical corpus.

Harim is a Hebrew personal or family name, rendered “Harim.” It identifies people or a group bearing that name rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs 11 times, mainly in Nehemiah and Ezra, and also once in 1 Chronicles. Because the available passages do not include their verse text here, the specific identity of each person or group cannot be determined from the name alone. Its meaning in any particular verse therefore comes from that passage’s surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “parched.” It describes something made dry, especially through the absence of moisture. In its only Old Testament occurrence, it functions as a description of the land in Jeremiah 17:6, presenting a condition rather than an action or person. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic sense is a land condition marked by dryness. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its normal biblical usage is represented by this single occurrence.

This word refers to a person called a “Hushathite.” It functions as a personal designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The Hebrew Old Testament uses it five times, and each occurrence is rendered “Hushathite.” It appears in passages naming or identifying individuals in the historical records of David’s mighty men and officials. The word’s precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense is the identification of someone as a Hushathite.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “lamb,” a young sheep. It is used twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in 1 Samuel 7:9 and once in Isaiah 65:25. In both places, it identifies the animal itself rather than an action or quality. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is simply a lamb.

Jeberechiah is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, and its English rendering is “Jeberechiah.” The available lexical information does not provide a separate descriptive definition for the name, so its ordinary sense is simply the person identified by this name. It appears in Isaiah 8:2; understanding that verse’s specific role requires the surrounding text.

It identifies people named Jehozabad in four Old Testament occurrences, appearing in Kings and Chronicles. The name functions as a proper designation for a person, so its significance comes from whom the passage names, not from an abstract concept. Its precise reference is determined by the individual passage in which it appears.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “sons.” It functions as a noun identifying sons in statements about a household or family. Its uses occur thirteen times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages concerning households, descendants, and those connected with a household. The word appears from Genesis through Jeremiah, showing a recurring family-related use rather than a term limited to one isolated passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name: “Jesse.” It identifies a specific person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. Its use appears in family-line and genealogical settings, including passages in Ruth, Samuel, and Chronicles, where Jesse is connected with birth and descent. The name occurs 42 times in the Hebrew Old Testament and retains the same naming function throughout those occurrences. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “Thus,” functioning adverbially to point to the manner, result, or form of something being stated or done. It often helps introduce or connect a statement, directing the reader to consider what follows in relation to what has already been said. It occurs 577 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise force is shaped by the surrounding sentence and passage. Its broad use makes it a connective word rather than a term naming a person, object, or action.

Calcol is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. It is rendered as “Calcol” and appears twice in the Old Testament corpus: once in 1 Kings 4:31 and once in 1 Chronicles 2:6. Since this is a name, its ordinary function is to identify a person; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific role in each passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “Letushim,” a name preserved in the genealogy of Abraham’s descendants. It functions as a name identifying a particular group in the biblical record, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Genesis 25:3, in a birth-and-genealogy setting. The available English renderings retain it as “Letushim,” so the name itself is the clearest meaning.

The Hebrew word means “sup.” In its only recorded occurrence, it functions as the expression rendered “sup” in the sentence, rather than as a broad or frequently repeated Bible term. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Habakkuk 1:9. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this entry establishes the word’s basic lexical sense without assigning further contextual meaning.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “instruction.” It refers to teaching intended to guide a person’s understanding and conduct. In the Old Testament, it is especially prominent in Proverbs, where instruction is connected with receiving wisdom and responding rightly to guidance. It can also describe instruction associated with God’s dealings with his people. The word occurs 50 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring emphasis on learning that shapes how a person lives.

Mishael is a Hebrew personal name, not a word that describes an action, quality, or object. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus represented here, it appears once, in Daniel 2:17, and the English rendering preserves it as “Mishael.” Because a personal name is being carried over rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive term, its role is to identify a particular person; the surrounding verse is needed to identify that person’s place in the passage.

This Hebrew word means “beam,” referring to a large, strong piece of timber. It is used as a noun for a substantial wooden object, rather than for a person, action, or abstract idea. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, each time in a separate verse. Its occurrences are found in 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles, showing a consistent meaning across these passages.

The Hebrew word means “influences.” It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job 38:31. In that occurrence, it functions as an object—the thing referred to as acted upon by the sentence’s verbs. Its ordinary lexical contribution is therefore a reference to influences, while the surrounding verse determines precisely what those influences are and how the statement presents them. No broader range of uses is represented in the Hebrew Scriptures.

This Hebrew word refers to “milk” as an action: it describes drawing nourishment from milk rather than naming the milk itself. It functions as a verb, expressing what people do when they receive milk in this way. The word therefore points to an act of feeding and nourishment, not merely to a substance. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 66:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse context.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “sheaf,” referring to a bundle of harvested grain stalks. It is a noun used for an agricultural bundle, naming a familiar harvest object rather than an action or quality. The word occurs five times in the Old Testament, in Genesis and Psalms. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage and its connection with the harvest scene.

This Hebrew word is rendered “for” and functions as an action word in Old Testament sentences. It appears 25 times across 24 verses, from Numbers through Lamentations. Its role is expressed through what a person or people do toward God or others, so the surrounding sentence is needed to understand its precise force each time. The word is especially associated with statements involving deliberate human action and its consequences, rather than with a person, place, or object.

Nezib is a Hebrew name rendered “Nezib.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at Joshua 15:43, and the English renderings preserve it as a name rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive word. The available wording does not provide enough context to explain more about the entity itself, so its clearest lexical sense is simply the proper name Nezib.

This Hebrew word means “rainy.” It functions as a description of weather associated with rain, rather than naming a person, object, or action. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Proverbs 27:15. The available rendering is consistent in identifying the word as “rainy,” giving a clear basic sense even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in Proverbs depends on that passage’s context.

This Hebrew word expresses helping: giving assistance or support to someone. In its only recorded Old Testament occurrence, it describes an action rather than a person, place, or object. Its English rendering is “helping,” so its central idea is active assistance. It appears once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 5:2; the surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly who is helping and how. The word itself does not establish the full circumstances without that context.

This word refers to the place-name “Sepharvaim.” It is not presented here with an ordinary descriptive definition; instead, its role is to identify a named place in the Old Testament. The name occurs seven times, in six verses, appearing in 2 Kings and Isaiah. English Bible renderings preserve it as “Sepharvaim,” confirming that it functions as a name rather than a translated description. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and account.

This word means to move away or depart. It describes something passing from one place or condition to another, and can also express the idea of something being changed or removed. The approved renderings “away” and “departed” capture its central sense. It occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel, so its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Accho is the name of a place. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Judges 1:31, and is rendered “Accho.” Because this word is a place-name rather than a common noun or action word, its meaning is primarily the identification of that location. The surrounding verse determines what is being said about Accho, but the word itself functions as a geographical name. Its recorded use is limited to that single occurrence.

This Hebrew word means “for,” functioning as a connecting term within a sentence. Its precise role can vary with the surrounding wording, so the word should be read as part of the complete clause rather than treated as a standalone idea. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job 20:18, Job 39:13, and Proverbs 7:18. Those references show that it is rare, and its meaning is best kept to this concise connective sense.

This Hebrew word refers to “branches,” the growth that extends outward from a tree or plant. It functions as a concrete term for part of a plant, rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 19:10. The surrounding verse text is not included here, so this cache explains the word’s ordinary lexical sense rather than its particular force in that passage.

This Hebrew word describes a person as destitute—lacking the resources or support needed for ordinary life. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Psalm 102:17, so its normal meaning is narrowly attested rather than broadly illustrated across many passages. The word functions as a description of needy condition, while the surrounding verse determines how that condition is presented. Its repeated English rendering is “destitute.”

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Asenath,” identifying a woman rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. It appears three times in the Old Testament, all in Genesis, where it functions as a person’s name in accounts involving family and genealogy. Its use remains consistent throughout its occurrences: it refers to Asenath herself. The surrounding passage supplies the particular details about her role, while the word’s ordinary meaning is simply this proper name.

Paruah is a Hebrew personal name, preserved as “Paruah” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Kings 4:17. Because it functions as a name, its meaning for readers is primarily identification: it identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or idea. The surrounding verse supplies the information needed to understand that person’s role there.

This word is the proper name “Perezuzza,” used as a specific name rather than as an ordinary descriptive term. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in two verses: 2 Samuel 6:8 and 1 Chronicles 13:11. The name is associated with the same recorded designation in both passages, while its precise significance in each verse depends on the surrounding verse text. It should therefore be read as a named reference, not expanded into an unsupported list of meanings.

This Hebrew word refers to a place named “Zelah.” It functions as a proper place name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Joshua 18:28 and once in 2 Samuel 21:14. Since it is consistently rendered “Zelah,” its meaning for a Bible reader is chiefly identification: it names a location mentioned in those passages, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific significance of that location.

“Kadesh” is a proper name used for a location in the Hebrew Old Testament. It identifies a place mentioned in connection with journeys, settlement, and boundaries. The name occurs 18 times, entirely within the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, with several occurrences in Numbers and Genesis. Because this word functions as a place-name, its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding context rather than from a general descriptive meaning.

Its role is therefore best understood simply as naming a spear within that passage.

This Hebrew verb means to tear or rend something apart. It describes an action in which a person or object is split, opened, or pulled apart, whether literally or as an expressive action. The word occurs 63 times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, showing that it is used across many passages rather than belonging to one narrow setting. Its normal sentence function is verbal: it expresses the act of tearing. The precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being torn and the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “proud,” describing someone marked by pride or self-exaltation. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 40:4. The available wording identifies it as a description of a proud person or group, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise force in that passage. Its recorded use is connected with actions directed toward it, showing that it functions as the object of those actions rather than as the action itself.

The word occurs 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Habakkuk. Its normal sense identifies creatures by their manner of movement rather than naming one particular species.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “palaces,” referring to grand or fortified residences. It is used for buildings connected with kings, cities, and places of prominence. The word occurs 32 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing especially in prophetic descriptions and accounts of royal or fortified places. Its normal function is to name these substantial buildings rather than the people who live in them. Context determines whether the reference emphasizes their strength, destruction, or public significance.

This Hebrew word means “seventh,” identifying something that comes in position seven within an ordered sequence. It is used for a numbered day, time, person, or other item, helping mark its place in relation to what comes before and after it. The word appears 98 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Zechariah, showing regular use for identifying the seventh position. Its exact significance in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “be,” expressing a state or condition in a sentence. It can describe someone or something existing in a particular position or condition, while the surrounding words establish the specific sense. The word occurs 20 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic function appears across several kinds of passages rather than belonging to one narrow setting. Its precise force in any verse depends on the sentence and surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to a cry. It appears only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Job, so its ordinary meaning is supported by a small number of passages. As a word, it functions to identify or express a cry rather than describe a broad range of actions or qualities. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, which are not included here. The clearest supported meaning is “cry.”

This Hebrew word means “deliver.” It is an action word describing rescue from danger, threat, or an overpowering situation. In its nine Old Testament occurrences, all found in Daniel, it consistently expresses the act of bringing someone out of peril. The word may describe what a ruler hopes or asks for, or what God is recognized as able to do. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding context.

The word refers to a “mantle,” functioning as a noun for something worn or used as a covering. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Judges 4:18. Because no verse text is provided here, its precise appearance and significance in that scene must be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the word alone. The available rendering identifies the object simply as a mantle, without supplying a broader range of meanings.

This Hebrew word refers to “steps”—the movements or course a person takes while walking. It is used of human conduct pictured as a path that can be kept, followed, turned from, or brought into difficulty. The word occurs 9 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Psalms and Job, where attention is given to the direction and condition of a person’s steps.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “tip.” It is used as a noun for the end or extremity of something. In its eight Old Testament occurrences, it appears in Exodus and Leviticus, especially in passages involving ritual actions. The word itself identifies the particular tip being addressed, while the surrounding passage determines its exact physical reference and significance. Its occurrences are concentrated in these priestly and cleansing instructions rather than spread broadly across the Old Testament.

This Hebrew word means “rise.” It functions as an action word, expressing that someone or something rises. In the Hebrew Bible, it appears once, at Psalm 139:21. Because this is its only recorded occurrence, the surrounding verse supplies the context for how the action is understood there, while the core meaning remains the act of rising. Its meaning is therefore focused and specific within the Hebrew corpus.
